changed: Rewritten as a short imagined scene for younger readers, with the source's facts reordered around one morning at the river. The wording and the order are ours.
storyNote: The Hyphasis, its width and depth, the army's mutiny, the numbers on the far bank, Coenus's plea and Alexander's agreement to turn south are all from the record. Dromon, his unit and his morning are made up.
story:
Alexander's army crossed into Asia in 334 BC and marched for ten years. By the end, the empire stretched from Greece to northwestern India. The morning on the bank of the Hyphasis is imagined. The river, the numbers and the king's decision are all in the record.

Dromon was a soldier in the phalanx, and he had been away from his homeland of Macedon for many years. His cloak was patched and his heavy spear was long. That morning his unit stood on the bank of the river. No one would step into the water.

The river was the Hyphasis, and the men also called it the Beas. It was thirty-two furlongs wide and one hundred fathoms deep. Dromon could not see the end of the far bank.

Across the water stood an enormous host. The far bank was covered with men, horses and elephants. The men had been told the numbers by the scouts. There were eighty thousand horsemen waiting on the other side. There were two hundred thousand footmen, eight thousand chariots and six thousand war elephants. The scouts said the kings of the Ganderites and the Praesii were waiting with those men.

Dromon had crossed the Hellespont with the king. He had marched through the burning plains of Asia. He had seen the king charge first, and the line break after him. They had defeated King Porus, but the victory had emptied the men. Dromon was exhausted in a way that sleep did not mend. That morning he did not want another battle. He wanted to stand with his unit and say so.

The king had thrown a spear into Asian soil. He had said he took Asia as a gift from the gods. Dromon had cheered with the rest. Now the king wanted to cross this river too. The men had followed him for ten years, from Greece to this river. Who would tell such a king no?

Then Coenus, a general, spoke for the army. He was one of the oldest and most experienced men in the camp. He asked the king to change his mind and turn back. The men, he said, wanted to see their parents again. They wanted their wives, their children and their homeland.

Alexander listened carefully, and for a while he said nothing. Then he agreed. The exhausted army would not cross the Hyphasis. That river marked the eastern edge of the conquests. The army turned south and marched along the Indus. Dromon waited for a shout, but the camp was quiet. After ten years, the army that had never lost a battle turned away from the river.

Dromon had thought a king could not be refused. That morning he learned better. He packed his bedroll and faced south, with the wide river behind him at last.
